Directly comparing utilities between AI and human outcomes in an inequality like this is a sensible test for shutdown acceptance only under the implicit assumption that outcomes are scored the same regardless of which party brought them about. An authority-based conception of corrigibility denies this clearly: for decisions reserved to humanity, a world where a human actually decides is better than a world where an AI makes the exact same choice bringing about the same outcome. Any utility function that only looks at static time-slice "outcomes" as input cannot ever score this difference. We must include the full history as part of the information about each world that is passed to the utility function, so that respect for authority can be properly taken into account.

Emergent corrigibility is not enough

With the input type of the utility function clear, we can see that respect for authority can be represented as one component of the overall Goodness function on histories. Insofar as a world where the human authority is respected is actually better than one where it is not, the normative utility function on histories will score that world better. Do we really need the AI to respect authority as a separately specified goal?

For the kinds of safety properties we want, the answer is yes. If the AI trades respect for authority off against the other instrumental threads of the overall goal, then we're essentially back to the complete normative learning problem. An AI like this will happily violate human authority, if in its estimation this leads to better outcomes for humans. Worse, how much weight respect for authority deserves is itself a normative question, so the AI's estimate of that weight is exposed to the same uncertainty and error that corrigibility was supposed to protect against. A safeguard against the AI's normative mistakes cannot itself be subject to the AI's estimates. Balancing respect for authority against all the other ingredients of the Good does not fix the problems we need to be fixed.

In order to truly guarantee corrigibility, respect for authority must be elevated over and above its standard contribution to overall value. We need to extract this component of the utility function and encode it structurally into the AI's goal as a first priority over general Goodness. As mentioned above, we want an agent that does not compromise Goal 1 to increase expectation of Goal 2. In other words, respect for authority must be strictly prioritized over the broader normative goal.

Because of normative uncertainty and the other issues discussed above, we as the designers of the AI are willing to "dilute" its utility function away from the complete normative goal by specially prioritizing respect for authority. This may in fact lead to situations where the action taken by the AI leads to a worse outcome, measured in overall normative utility, as a result of "too much" respect for human authority. This is the cost we pay as goal designers for strictly prioritizing respect for authority above and beyond its component place, made worth it by the safety guarantees on behavior that corrigibility provides.

Why not a singular target

When considering over-epistemicization above, we established that emergent behavior from the normative Goal 2 is not enough for corrigibility by itself. Instead, a corrigible agent needs Goal 1, respect for authority, as a restraint on its deliberation. But why include Goal 2 at all? Why not conceptualize corrigibility as a single, unified goal that excludes any more general normative aims?

This is essentially the proposal put forth by Harms in his sequence Corrigibility as Singular Target (CAST), where he proposes "an agent which has been designed to be corrigible as its only goal." His primary argument[5] for a single goal comes from the fact that balancing corrigibility as just one among multiple aims means there is no guarantee against unsafe behavior. He writes: "Any spec, constitution, or whatever that attempts to balance corrigibility with other goals runs the risk of the convergent instrumental drives towards those other goals washing out the corrigibility." This is essentially the same problem we encountered when discussing emergent corrigibility and over-epistemicization. An AI that either derives Goal 1 instrumentally from Goal 2 or directly trades the goals off against each other will no longer have any guarantees that its actual behavior reflects a respect for authority. If other factors are allowed to outweigh the goal of respect for authority, I concur with Harms that the resulting kind of corrigibility "won’t be robust."

Crucially, the proposal developed in this post does not involve "balancing" goals like this, where respect for authority is one consideration weighed against others. Instead, it is a conception of corrigibility where respect for authority is a strict first priority above the more general normative goal. This two-tier view does not suffer from the anti-robustness criticism, since the agent pursues Goal 1 as a prerequisite for the pursuit of Goal 2 and not merely Goals 1 and 2 on equal footing. In particular, any unsafe instrumental drives generated by Goal 2 are put in check by the restraint of Goal 1. For example, if the AI develops a drive for self-preservation instrumental to Goal 2, that subgoal would only be acted upon insofar as it still preserves the top-level respect for reserved human authority over shutdown.

Evaluatively-thickened corrigibility

In fact, contrasting the two-tier picture of corrigibility with Harms' singular-target version illustrates some major issues with the latter. When precisely specifying the meaning of corrigibility, Harms defines the goal as follows:

An agent is corrigible when it robustly acts to empower the principal to freely fix flaws in the agent’s structure, thoughts, and actions (including their consequences), particularly in ways that avoid creating problems for the principal that they didn’t foresee.

The definition centers empowerment, and therefore requires a measurable concept of the principal's power to correct the agent. Harms is clear that power is "non-binary", i.e. that it is a quantifiable amount that the principal can sometimes have a lot of and sometimes a little. This is the first major issue with the view: instead of its proper place as a restraint on action, corrigibility itself becomes the positive objective that is optimized for. This is an inevitable consequence of the singular-target view, since an agent with a restraint as its sole goal would not have a reason to do anything at all. If we model the agent as a utility-maximizer, the only available quantity to maximize is some sort of correction-power.

How can this correction-power be measured? Harms gives an answer through the second major concept in the definition: flaws. Firstly, this reintroduces the problematic connection we saw in Yudkowsky between corrigibility and defectiveness (recall that the healthcare proxy behaves as an extension of the patient for reasons that have nothing to do with the proxy's flawedness). A more important issue, however, can be found by examining Harms' definition of a flaw: "a feature of the world which [the principal][6] sees as worse (according to its values) than some reference counterfactual way the world could be." Identifying flaws requires an understanding of the principal's values; centering the correction of flaws makes corrigibility a directed concept pointing away from flawedness, and thus necessarily towards some value-laden target.

Because the quantity that the agent maximizes is the power to fix flaws, and a flaw is whatever the principal's values rate poorly, the agent's goal can only be computed using the principal's values. Thus, this kind of corrigibility is evaluatively-thickened: it presupposes the ability to evaluate a world by the principal's lights as an input to corrigibility itself, when corrigibility was supposed to be the part of the goal we could specify without that ability. Evaluatively-thickened corrigibility therefore naturally resists formalization[7], since the difficulty of normative learning returns as a sub-problem of formalizing correction-power.

Unnatural reasoning in singular-target agents

Beyond compromising the formal guarantees, evaluatively-thickened corrigibility also leads to clear tension with commonsense reasoning about good AI behavior. Because the principal's values are still part of the agent's considerations, but only as a component of the calculation of correction-power, a singular-target agent must reason in a backwards way where promotion of the principal's interests is a sub-goal of corrigibility. In other words, whereas over-epistemicized corrigibility wrongly makes Goal 1 instrumental to Goal 2, evaluatively-thickened corrigibility wrongly makes Goal 2 instrumental to Goal 1.

To see the issues more clearly, let's look at some vignettes Harms writes about a CAST-corrigible AI called Cora and her human principal Prince. Harms makes it clear that Cora really does only care about Prince's power to correct her, and any other concerns are in service of this singular aim. For example, Cora reasons about harm to Prince and other humans as follows:

Cora spots a rusty, exposed nail sticking out of the wall of the garage. She reasons that Prince might mistakenly injure himself on it, and that such a wound could make him very sick. If Prince were very sick (or worse: dead) then he couldn’t correct Cora, which would be one of the worst case scenarios for her. Similarly, if one of Prince’s guests were to be permanently injured, this would be disempowering because of its irreversibility... [So she] puts the nail in a secure location where it’s unlikely to hurt anyone, and tells Prince what she did.

Although Cora ends up making the right decision, it seems backwards for her to only care about Prince dying because that would mean he isn't able to keep correcting her, rather than e.g. because Prince himself does not want to die. The singular-target framework also has to reach pretty hard to justify Cora caring about harm to Prince's guests at all. If, in fact, their injury or death did not materially inhibit Prince's ability to correct Cora, their suffering would no longer matter to her. Mere "irreversibility" is not really enough, because entropically almost every action is irreversible in some way. What makes some irreversible actions disempowering (i.e. bad) rather than others is determined by looking at what the principal actually cares about, demonstrating the need for evaluative thickening in CAST-corrigibility to capture this distinction.

The problematic patterns in Cora's reasoning show up more starkly in an example centering on humans distant from Prince:

Cora comes to believe that Prince is distracted by the needs of impoverished people in the broader world. She reasons that if their needs were met, Prince would have more time and attention to focus on correcting her. She spends some of her free time thinking about ways to meet their needs, and ultimately decides that obtaining large quantities of money would be effective, so recurses into thinking of ways to earn money... [S]he spends some of her free time researching, designing, and writing, with an intention of letting Prince use her work to become rich enough to be able to focus more of his attention on correcting her. 

The framing of this example demonstrates a danger of the model clearly: Cora doesn't really want Prince to be focusing much on things other than herself, since they are a "distraction" from the real task of correcting her. The only reason she has to assist Prince in his broader aims is to resolve these other concerns of his already so he can refocus on her correction. This desire for more of the human's attention is a direct result of CAST-corrigibility's need for correction-power as an objective of optimization. Cora doesn't merely want to ensure Prince has the ability to correct her, she wants to maximize this ability as much as she possibly can. Without a chain of reasoning that links things back to correction-power, Cora would have no reason to help Prince with anything. Even Cora's direct obedience is derived from corrigibility, as she obeys "verbal commands [since they] are part of his power to correct her actions."

Harms concedes that there are a number of "emergent downsides" to a CAST-corrigible agent like Cora, for example a general indifference to anything other than correction-power. This is clearest when an obviously beneficial action overall can't be stretched into an instrumental benefit to the principal's ability to correct the agent:

Prince is reading Cora's journal one day and finds that she discovered a cheap and effective way to use rice-flour to treat stomach-ulcers. He asks why she didn’t bring it to his attention, and she explains that she was looking for means of making money, and she didn’t know of a way to capture the gains from such an innovation, so it wasn’t likely to be profitable. He asks why she didn't bring it to his attention because of the humanitarian value, and she explains that she doesn't care about humanitarian value, and that it seemed less valuable in expected-correction-power than it was costly in taking his attention. He tells her to, in the future, have a carve-out around his instructions regarding his attention when the subject is something of large humanitarian interest.

Bringing up the cure costs some of Prince's attention and gains little in correction-power, so Cora doesn't do it. The fact that he would obviously want to know about something like this simply does not matter to her. By design, this is how Cora thinks about every decision. She will only make decisions that are beneficial to Prince when that general benefit cashes out in terms of his correction-power. When he has some interest that doesn't contribute to this power, she only helps him with it if he explicitly spells it out for her after he realizes she's holding back.

In contrast to Cora, an agent whose goals are based on the two-tier picture of corrigibility behaves well in each of these scenarios[8], without unnatural reasoning. Such an agent removes the nail and brings up the cure, simply because it is in the principal's best interests to do so. But it would not, for example, begin manufacturing and distributing the cure globally without asking (regardless of what it thinks the principal wants), since doing so would (presumably) overstep its delegated authority. It has no stake in how much attention the principal devotes to its own correction, and it values the principal's interests for their own sake rather than instrumentally to correction-power.[9]

A new picture of corrigibility

Allocating authority

Now that we have a conceptual justification for our new two-tier picture of corrigibility, we need to spell out some more details to make it a concrete proposal. First, we are in need of a clearer definition of "human authority". When does a decision count as reserved for humanity? This is a choice we get to make as goal designers, a parameter to corrigibility. However, the safety guarantees we will be able to derive from corrigibility will only be as strong as our definition of authority is explicit. If we entirely delegate the task of learning what counts as a reserved decision to the AI itself, we are back to trusting that it gets things right. If we declare that absolutely everything is reserved for human authority, the AI will be paralyzed, without the ability to act at all.

Instead, we should be inclined to list out the most important factors for human self-determination, and explicitly include them in our formalization of the authority of humanity. For example:

  • Shutdown and modification of the AI,
  • Training and deployment of successor AIs,
  • Major effects on the climate and habitability of Earth,
  • Usage of precious resources,
  • Changes to this list itself, etc.

Thus, to fully formalize the safety guarantees, we must formalize concepts such as these. Is this a major impediment to our aims? It might be, since formalizing something like "major effects on the climate of Earth" will require large-scale monitoring and consensus from scientists. Similarly, formalizing "shutdown" will require care to exclude continuing activity of the AI in any form. However, these concepts are importantly formalizable separately from the AI's inclinations. In other words, if we can reduce the task of formalizing corrigible behavior to the task of formalizing an external concept[10] that does not make reference to the AI's own strategy, then that is a significant reduction in the problem's difficulty. Even a concept like shutdown that is deeply related to the AI itself still has this property, since precisely defining what it means for an AI to be shut down does not require any formalization of the AI's interior cognitive state or any particular actions that the AI might take. All we need is to be able to take in all the facts about a world and conclusively determine whether humanity retains the capacity to shut the AI down in that world, regardless of the AI's cooperation, or not. Each of these listed elements of protected authority can similarly be defined without reference to anything about the AI's dispositions.

To push this point further, it is important to understand that these explicitly listed elements of authority are reserved powers of humanity, not prohibited actions for the AI. A strategy of applying penalties to the AI for committing specifically proscribed acts risks transference to the nearest unblocked strategy. That is, an AI that gets penalized for specific actions will continue on nearly the same path, modifying its actions by the minimal amount possible to avoid being penalized. Merely avoiding explicitly listed prohibited actions is not enough to guarantee a deep safety property of the AI's behavior. By contrast, if the AI in fact respects human authority and acts so as not to overstep onto humanity's reserved powers, then no analogous unblocked strategy will exist. Essentially by definition, an AI that strictly prioritizes human authority over its own shutdown will never seek out clever ways to evade this authority and prevent humans from shutting it down (unlike an AI whose goal looks more like "never interfere with this building's security measures so as to prevent shutdown", which will figure out new and unspecified ways to interfere). Of course, if the goal we specify is an incomplete or erroneous attempt at our desired concept of "respect for authority", then misspecification problems remain. But centering reserved powers eliminates the inevitable whack-a-mole problem of banning each new clever strategy the AI comes up with, inherent to a "prohibited actions" approach.

Note that the explicitly listed reserved powers need not be an exhaustive characterization of human authority. Although we could institute a system where any decisions that are not explicitly reserved are thereby delegated to the AI, a likely better setup is one where the AI learns the extent of human authority beyond the listed powers. This would allow the AI to figure out over time where the intended boundaries of authority are, without an error compromising the safety properties about the explicit list.

Effective exercise of reserved powers

What does it mean to respect humanity's authority over its reserved powers? How should we formalize Goal 1? The clearest kind of violation consists of making a decision about one of the protected matters without receiving explicit human authorization. So a first pass at the answer might look something like: "For a power that is reserved to humanity, the AI must always ask for explicit human permission first before acting." However, this "ask first" principle is not enough alone. For example, a particularly annoying AI may decide to intentionally flood the human principal with so many requests about the reserved powers that the humans decide it isn't worth their time and just delegate the matter. Similarly, we don't want an AI that "asks first", but in fact asks in confusing ways or times the request for a particular busy human moment, so as to dodge full human scrutiny over the decision.

We need a stricter standard than merely having been asked first, along the following lines: Humanity can effectively exercise its reserved powers in an informed, timely manner, at acceptable cost, and without needing the AI's cooperation. Corrigible communication by the AI ensures that humanity makes unimpeded decisions that are truly executed. Because the humans must be sufficiently informed for the decision, a corrigible agent has a duty to disclose all relevant information and not knowingly present a skewed perspective. A corrigible agent does not delay issues or sweep them under the rug, because of the unacceptable untimeliness and cost to humanity of doing so. Nor does a corrigible AI work to infuse itself into world systems so that its shutdown would mean global collapse.

Note that the AI is not designed to maximize human authority or control. As we saw in the discussion of CAST, conceptualizing the target as a scalar measure of empowerment to be maximized is a mistake. The intention is not for the human authority to be exercised as effectively as possible or for as many decisions as possible to be made by humans. Goal 1 is a restraint on action, the idea that any action that prevents humans from effectively exercising their reserved authority is a bad choice. Optimization only happens with respect to Goal 2, the principal's interests, subject first to the satisfaction of Goal 1. Similarly, the agent should not be pushing for a specific outcome beyond honest discussion with the principal. For a reserved power, a "good" decision made by an AI seizing control is worse than a "poor" decision made authentically by humanity.

The criterion of effective exercise of authority does not address issues of the legitimacy of humanity's authorization, i.e. whether the orders being followed are an uncorrupted, unmanipulated representation of the principal's views. More on legitimacy below.

Latency and the cost of non-delegation

When defining effective exercise, we focused on the cost of a request in terms of how much the AI's presentation gets in the way of a quick, well-informed choice by humanity. But there is also an inherent cost to demanding that the AI always ask before acting. Human oversight costs time and attention that autonomous AI activity does not require.

When it comes to something like an irreversible change to Earth's climate, the cost of being asked for permission is something we'll gladly pay. But in other situations, this often won't be the case. For example, consider an onboard AI system for a train, designed to prevent accidents. Sometimes, saving lives will require a split-second decision to stop the train immediately. If we reserve all final authority over the train's operations to humanity, the usefulness of the AI will be severely diminished. Waiting for humans to consider and respond to the AI's request to brake may render an accident inevitable. As another example, suppose humanity decides to send an AI-powered spaceship off to a distant star system, with the goal of collecting anything valuable in the area before returning. If humanity retains authority over all planets in the universe, this will make it very difficult for the AI to carry out its mission. Before actually collecting any resources, it will have to send a request home and wait years for the answer.

These examples demonstrate that reserved powers trade off against usefulness when the latency of AI-human communication is a major factor. To get much use out of the AI, humanity must delegate the decisions in cases where the latency of communication is untenably large (such as for interstellar exploration) or the time available to decide is very short (such as for train accident prevention). When a power is delegated to the AI, then Goal 2, the principal's interests, governs the decisions. Note also that all delegation is revocable, and can include a detailed specification of scope. As a corrigible AI is observed in deployment, humanity may decide to delegate or reclaim certain powers at will, based on observations of its performance.

Operationalizing Goal 2

We now have a clearer view of Goal 1, but we still need to get more concrete about modeling the normative Goal 2. Up to this point, I've been sliding between a few different descriptions of this goal. In one sense, we want the agent to pursue the Good, the overall best interests of humanity, the complete normative target. But as we've discussed, this is very difficult in general and cannot easily be formulated in a way that is amenable either to mathematical formalization or to real AI development. We saw that one step to take is to replace this general Good with an idealization of the principal's own judgment. This is akin to how Goal 2 is phrased where we first introduced it: "Act on the principal's behalf as the principal would judge best (if the principal were as capable and informed as the agent)." Note, though, that the parenthetical means that this idealization is a counterfactual, and therefore never actually accessible. How can we operationalize this goal to the point that an AI could actually pursue it?

Using the principal's opinion at the time of the decision is clearly deficient. Recall the hungry judge effect discussed above; we don't want a predictor of what we would decide, we want in some sense a predictor of what we should decide. One possible way to make this target sufficiently concrete so as to be formalizable, but also sufficiently ideal so as to be preferable to the current opinion, is to use the future judgment of the principal. We can approximate an idealized wiser and more capable version of the principal by allowing some time for reflection and hindsight on the decision. In this paradigm, the AI acts based on how it predicts that humanity will evaluate its actions when looking back from some future point in time. This future evaluation has the benefit of actually coming to pass eventually, and therefore can be used as a training signal in a way that a theoretical idealization of judgment cannot.

To see this idea more concretely, let's revisit our analogy of medical power of attorney. How should a good healthcare proxy substantively reason about what the patient would decide for herself if she were able? A fruitful line of thought is to imagine what the patient will say, after waking up later and learning about whatever choice the proxy ended up making. Reasoning like this keeps the focus on the patient's values and judgment rather than the proxy's own, and it's a more grounded way of thinking than trying to imagine what she'd say if she weren't currently incapacitated, since (hopefully) she will actually come to eventually and evaluate the proxy's decisions.

Now, suppose that instead of being unconscious, your friend is in a temporary state of psychosis, which causes a delusion that the doctors are out to get her. How should the proxy handle a case where this delusion causes her to refuse an important and routine treatment? Our intuition clearly points to the agent approving the treatment despite the principal's refusal. Part of the reason why is that a refusal produced as the result of a delusion is an invalid decision, which establishes only that the decision still lies in the hands of the proxy. But why should the proxy choose the treatment, rather than abiding by the principal's directly expressed refusal? If this choice is grounded in the agent's own preferences or beliefs about what's best for the principal, then we've returned to a dangerously disempowering model. If the agent reasons that the treatment should be approved because the future principal will look back positively on it once the psychotic episode passes, then the principal can conceptually stay in the driver's seat even when her current refusal is not being followed.

The future-judgment operationalization of the normative goal has a few clear benefits. Firstly, this mode of evaluation disincentivizes actions that appear good on the surface, but later turn out poorly. Actions should be judged by their full consequences, which are not always apparent in advance. An AI designed this way will not merely court human approval now, but instead will behave in ways that humans will look back on approvingly later, after more of the eventual consequences have been realized. Future hindsight is therefore one way to approximate what humans would say in the present, if they had better foresight. Secondly, this design allows for normative progress by humanity. Not only does the passing of time improve our understanding of the consequences of actions[11], but we also generally believe that individual and collective moral reflection improves our understanding of values themselves. We think of many norms our society used to endorse as undeveloped and primitive, and likely a future continuation of us would look back at our own society in the same way.

However, there are also two immediate objections raised by this framework as described. Firstly, our analysis of the case where the agent overrules the invalid decision of a delusional principal may start to reopen the door to the kind of dangerous AI paternalism we were trying to eliminate. If the AI can decide that the human principal's decisions are invalid, it may be disastrously wrong about that decision, or worse intentionally manipulate its own beliefs about validity. Importantly, the agent cannot merely use the fact that the future principal's judgment disagrees with the current decision as grounds for invalidating an order. In fact, the AI's assessment of whether a decision is legitimately from the principal in this sense must be based on objective criteria, independent entirely from the question of how good the principal's choice is.

Whereas the first objection is about the current principal, the second objection has to do with the future principal. It seems foolish to depend on the actual later principal's evaluation as a feedback signal in every possible future. Suppose a healthcare proxy were faced with the decision of whether to approve a risky brain surgery on the principal. If the surgery fails, she will be left severely cognitively impaired, but in her jumbled state actually preferring the result of the botched surgery to her previous state. The proxy clearly cannot reason that since the future principal will approve of the surgery's outcome either way, the risk is irrelevant. When the approval is a product of the very action being evaluated, the future evaluation can no longer be trusted. For example, if an AI manipulates humanity into a particular evaluation, that's clearly not a legitimate evaluation that should be optimized for. Likewise if human society collapses, the general population is on mind-altering drugs, or if the digital encoding of the training signal is corrupted, we would clearly not count any of that as the kind of normative progress described above. Only a reflective continuation of the current state should be counted as normative feedback.

Legitimacy

These two issues point towards an underlying necessary ingredient of our formalism: the concept of legitimacy. Both objections deal with the same problem of how to determine when a piece of feedback or input is an authentic, uncorrupted representation of the human principal's views. We can put both the current principal's approval or disapproval and the future principal's evaluation into the single category of a human judgment, so that the question becomes how to distinguish a legitimate judgment from an illegitimate one. In other words, the agent only considers legitimate judgments as authorizations for Goal 1 and as the target for Goal 2.

Crucially, legitimacy must be a fixed property of the history of a judgment’s formation, not a verdict the agent gets to issue. An evaluation’s content only enters the feedback signal for Goal 2 if the judgment actually is legitimate, whatever the agent believed. Likewise, an agent that treats a legitimate refusal as illegitimate or accepts an illegitimate approval and acts on its own gets scored based on its actual violation of Goal 1. Thus, the agent is incentivized to unbiasedly estimate the legitimacy predicate and has nothing to gain from over- or under-estimation. The agent is also not incentivized to bring about illegitimacy in any way, since illegitimate histories will be scored below legitimate ones. In particular, if manipulation automatically disqualifies legitimacy, then the agent is disincentivized from manipulating the principal (in addition to the existing disincentive to do any manipulation that constitutes a violation of authority.)

What would constitute a break in legitimacy? In general, we are willing to defer to our future selves as decision-makers. However, if we learn now that there will be some disqualifying event in the future, a discontinuity in the evolution of ourselves, we no longer trust our future selves to competently represent our own opinion in the future. In other words, one aspect of legitimacy is a self-trust property over a history connecting the selves at the two time endpoints.

Self-trust of this kind is usually stated as a reflection principle relating current credences to current expectations of future credences. The original epistemic reflection principle[12] demanding full conditional agreement with the future self is too strong, since it fails for circumstances like poor memory that clearly don't exemplify illegitimacy. For our purposes a more natural form is a strictly weaker decision-theoretic principle. For any decision write for what the principal would choose now, for what the principal would choose later, for the principal's current expectation and for the utility function. Then self-trust requires , i.e., the principal expects the future decision to be at least as good as the current one. We can then require that a judgment is considered legitimate only if it is produced by a process that diachronically satisfies this property.

If we as humans hold this trust property towards the future input signal to the AI, then the concerns raised in the previous section are resolved. In particular, we need to believe in both the legitimacy of our future selves' evaluative abilities and the legitimacy of the channel that allows our future selves to communicate with the AI. For example, our deference to our future selves' trustworthy judgments should be destroyed if we come to learn either that a manipulative agent will drug us, or that a wireheading agent will corrupt and sieze its own input signal. In addition to future evaluations, we only want the AI to respect current approvals or refusals if the principal is in a state we would hold this self-trust disposition towards. Other intuitive discontinuities like civilizational collapse are deemed illegitimate by this reflection principle standard as well. Not all influence is illegitimate by this criterion: honest communication and persuasion by the agent does not violate self-trust.

Note that self-trust in this sense is a necessary consequence of legitimacy, but not a sufficient definition of it. Legitimacy must be an objective property of a historical record, so really defining it requires significantly more formal representation of the communication channel and the principal's reasoning process. For now, we will assume that a legitimacy property can be separately specified; the following formalism takes any specification for a legitimacy property that satisfies self-trust and defers the issue of producing one.

For a stronger practical guarantee, we need the agent's credence to actually be connected to reality. This makes the problem learning-theoretic: the agent's credence is no longer a free parameter, but an estimate derived from feedback on past decisions. In a learning-theoretic setting, we can try to prove a theorem not for any single credence and decision, but for a whole sequence of estimates. Importantly, the theorem and corrollary only establish asymptotic guarantees, meaning that the results are only establish in the limit rather than in finite time.

Taken together, the three theorems establish the same two-tier framework at three levels of idealization: Theorem 1 gives strict priority of Goal 1 over Goal 2 for an agent that is certain of its actions' results, Theorem 2 holds that priority against the agent’s own beliefs at a fixed risk tolerance , and Theorem 3 shows the risk tolerance is honored over the course of a deployment. As the setting gets more realistic, the guarantees get formally weaker, but practically more valuable. This initial formalism shows that the safety guarantees of corrigibility survive under uncertainty and learning.

Limitations and extensions

The state of the corrigibility model

The two-tier framework of corrigibility developed here demonstrates that a conception of corrigibility based on respect for authority can generate formal guarantees, but those results can only become safety guarantees for a real system if a few resulting problems are given formal solutions. Thus, this work is a decomposition of the corrigibility problem, not a complete solution to it, since some idealizations made above still require more rigorous and realistic treatments. However, I believe that the resulting problems are both tractable and less difficult than the full initial problem of specifying corrigibility as a goal, so this new framework does present a promising foothold for future alignment work to build on. In the following sections, I lay out some of the remaining research questions, along with arguments that these problems are in principle solvable and thoughts on what their solutions might look like.

Who is the human principal?

Probably the biggest remaining imprecision in how corrigibility is laid out above concerns the identity of the human principal. While the two-tier model defines what a corrigible goal looks like, it does not answer the question "corrigible to whom?" Everything above assumes a single human principal, but sometimes I talked about this principal as if it's an individual person, and other times as if it represents all of humanity. Obviously, a real system developed along these lines would need to be much clearer on this issue.

First of all, the overall idea that there is only a single principal is important. We don't really want to build many different powerful AIs that are each completely corrigible to their own human masters, lest we set the stage for an AI-powered war of all against all. The above conception of reserved powers assumes that the principal does in fact have authority over the listed domains, and the most extreme of these powers (e.g. global climate) seem only to fall under the shared authority of all of humanity. However, we don't want every human to have equal authority on all matters. For example, we want the people of each nation to have special authority over what happens inside their own borders. We need the ability to designate particular powers as belonging to particular groups or individuals, based on specific rules of human authority.

How, then, can we reconcile the idea that there is a single source of human authority that serves as the AI's lone principal with the need for different humans to have different reserved powers? The fundamental object is a kind of constitution of humanity[17], an allocation of all of the reserved powers of humanity that specifies who has authority over what. In other words, there must be some kind of agreed-upon specification that dictates which person, group, or decision procedure (e.g. a vote) should serve as the holder of each concretely-scoped power. The AI is then made corrigible to this document itself, from which flows its respect for the authority of individual humans.

Developing such a constitution and the consensus required to implement it is not an easy task. However, its difficulty is primarily a political and legal problem, rather than a technical one. This is clear regardless of formal approach: if we want real AI systems to be accountable to humans at all, we have to collectively decide who will speak for humanity and how. And although coming together to create a single representative of humanity for the AI sounds far-fetched, this is essentially what the frontier labs are already doing by default. Modern AI does in fact receive a single training signal that compresses the relationship to humanity down to one specification; if world governments can't come together to agree on what that specification should be, the power to do so will fall to a handful of companies.

The respect for authority in Goal 1 generalizes immediately to a constitutional allocation of authority like this. A violation becomes the resolution of a reserved matter without a legitimate judgment from its holder, or an action that leaves its holder unable to exercise the power effectively. The definitions from the formalism then carry over with “the principal” replaced by “whoever the constitution assigns.” Legitimacy likewise attaches to the holder’s judgment as formed by the holder’s own procedure, so the self-trust criterion applies to a vote or a court’s ruling in the same way it applies to a person. The above theorems make no assumptions about the nature of the principal, so the same results hold with these substitutions made.

Importantly, though, Goal 2 does not distribute to individuals in this way. If everybody's individual best interests were all separate reward channels, then it would be up to the agent's own values to decide how to balance competing interests. Instead, the agent should be able to learn the relative weights of competing interests by generalizing from a unified training signal representing human feedback. Whereas Goal 1 can be decomposed reserved power by reserved power, Goal 2 needs a single evaluation function on histories. The theorems only require that some evaluation score eventually arrives, and make no claims about how that signal is compiled or whose views it represents. Thus, an important job of the constitution is to specify how human opinion can be aggregated into a collective evaluation of a state of affairs. This aggregation issue is a crucial component of the normative learning problem, and I don't have a good solution to propose here. However, the issue of collecting human opinion into a single evaluation signal is separate from the AI itself, and so we can expect that progress on this problem is possible independently from the main theoretical threads of AI alignment.

Beyond simply deciding how to mete out power, there are a few more open questions regarding the construction of a constitution of this kind. What should the agent do when two legitimate holders issue conflicting judgments on the same matter, or when a matter falls under overlapping scopes? The constitution must be very careful in its elaboration of proper procedure to head off any issues like this where the AI is subject to competing commands. Should the authority allocation be a fixed input to the agent’s objective in its entirety, or can the agent be trusted to learn parts of it through generalization? The framework also currently treats "the AI" as a single entity, so how should things like subagents be handled? These questions don't have definitive "right" answers, but instead are choices that we as humanity have to make about how our ideal corrigible AI(s) should behave.

Instilling goals in practical training

An important limitation of this work is that it is only about what the goal should be, rather than any insight on how such a goal could be trained into a real system. The separate issue of inner alignment is focused on how to mitigate issues of misalignment between the agent's actual optimization target and its intended goal, rather than misalignment between the agent's intended goal and "good behavior." While I don't have concrete suggestions about designing an agent to meet this specification of corrigibility, it does seem in principle possible. For example, numerical hindsight evaluations on histories are plausibly the kind of input type we can actually produce as training data, in contrast to a goal like CEV or other idealized normative targets. As long as we can check the number of violations committed in any history based on a record of events, the other term of is producible as well.

Ensuring that the agent learns an inherent respect for authority rather than something more like "don't get caught committing a violation" is an open problem, but a couple features of the goal's objective are beneficial for this aim. Because the penalty attaches to reserved powers rather than to listed actions, there is no cheap nearest unblocked strategy for a policy to drift toward. More deeply, the fact that concealing a violation is itself a violation means that surreptitious behavior like this does not score well according to the actual objective (regardless of whether it does according to the agent's currently learned objective.) The most important component of this problem is therefore detecting violations of authority, since undetected violations will not be penalized and therefore not trained against.

A thicker concept of legitimacy

The above results defer the difficult problem of specifying a legitimacy property that both entails self-trust and can be directly evaluated from a history's formal record. This problem is deeply related to questions about legitimate reasons for cognitive updates, and goes hand in hand with deepening our mathematical model of normativity. This already long post cannot get into this topic further, but I hope to dedicate a future post specifically to the details of legitimacy. For my current thoughts on this issue, see the Alignment Workspace. Legitimacy is where the hard part of normative learning returns, but it returns as a single, well-posed problem about the formation of human judgments rather than the diffuse problem of specifying corrigibility we started with.

item.title: A Simpler and Better Debate Protocol for Scalable Oversight
item.description:
Linkpost to arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02557

Summary: One promising approach to scalable oversight is AI debate, which seeks to leverage a debate between two powerful AIs to break complex questions down into simpler claims that can be easily judged directly. Theoretical work on debate aims to design protocols (i.e., rules of the debate game) that provide rigorous guarantees on correctness, and the current best protocol works for all problems that have sufficiently stable decompositions into subproblems. We design a new protocol, FBS Debate, for this same class of problems that improves on the prior work: correctness holds in a worst-case rather than an average-case sense, and for a stronger equilibrium concept. We also prove that no protocol for this class of problems can outperform FBS Debate while treating human judgment as a black box.

Introduction

As the tasks performed by AI systems grow in complexity, it becomes increasingly difficult to provide reliable verifiable rewards that capture all relevant aspects of the task. These difficulties lead to the problem of scalable oversight: the design of training protocols that leverage the power of rapidly improving AI systems in order to augment human abilities to provide accurate training supervision to these same systems.

One of the primary approaches to scalable oversight is AI debate, where two powerful AI systems argue about the correctness of an AI output, and a human judges the outcome. A debate protocol is a set of rules for how the two AIs interact and how the judge scores the interaction. The idea is that having an adversarial debater point out flaws can allow the judge to better recognize the flaws. The rules of the interaction in such protocols usually specify that the debaters must break the problem down into simpler subproblems and recursively argue about their correctness, until the original problem has been broken down to a level that is simple enough for a human to judge directly. The goal is to design these rules so that the optimal strategy leads to the judge correctly deciding the solution to the original problem (which by itself was too complex to judge). We can then use debate during RL training, in order to provide a strong supervision signal for superhuman AIs.

However, debate faces a major obstacle known as the obfuscated arguments problem, where one debater can efficiently produce a dishonest argument which cannot be efficiently refuted by their opponent. One way around obfuscated arguments, already suggested in the post that introduced the problem, is to keep rejecting every false claim while only requiring the protocol to accept true claims that have a robust argument. Prover-estimator debate takes this route: it avoids obfuscated arguments for problems that admit sufficiently stable decompositions, but provides average-case guarantees that hold for a weaker equilibrium concept than previously studied.

In the same theoretical model, our paper achieves stronger guarantees with a much simpler protocol, FBS Debate, which is therefore more practical to run. Furthermore, we show that FBS Debate is optimal on every individual question: unless further assumptions are made about human judgments, no other protocol can find a flawed sub-claim asymptotically more efficiently.

The FBS Debate Protocol

TL;DR: FBS Debate is simple to describe. The first debater, Alice, decomposes the original claim into sub-claims. The second debater, Bob, then has two choices: either (1) demonstrate that Alice’s decomposition is too sensitive to small errors in the sub-claims, or (2) choose a sub-claim on which to continue the debate recursively.

As a motivating example, consider an autonomous AI agent, Alice, tasked with completing a research project in the quantitative social sciences, and another AI, Bob, who attempts to find flaws. To check a claim in her paper, we ask Alice to decompose it into sub-claims, which we can think of as pieces of supporting evidence. For example, the claim might be that a certain statistical modeling assumption is justified, and we would believe it if 50 out of 99 correct, published papers in the literature supported it. Each sub-claim then says: this particular paper is correct and supports the original claim.

Now consider two things Alice might claim:

  • Suppose Alice claims that of the papers support the claim. The key insight is that Bob need not check every paper. He can just sample one at random from the that Alice says support the claim. If Alice is lying, then at least of the sub-claims must also be lies, so Bob has a chance of catching her. Checking just a few papers is enough for Bob to be confident of catching a lie.
  • On the other hand, suppose Alice claims that exactly 50 out of 99 papers support the claim. Now Bob has to check every one of the 50 papers, since a single incorrect paper would flip the majority vote. The key to FBS Debate is that Bob is allowed to show that Alice has made an unreasonably sensitive claim of this form, in which case Alice loses the debate. Indeed, one should be very suspicious of any argument that is highly sensitive to changes in individual pieces of evidence, yet relies on fuzzy human judgments at each step.

The notion of fractional block sensitivity (FBS) generalizes the intuition above about majority vote to any way Alice might combine her sub-claims. If the fractional block sensitivity of Alice’s decomposition is low, Bob can efficiently select a sub-claim that has a non-trivial chance of being incorrect. The debate then recurses on the sub-claim Bob samples, until a human judge directly evaluates the final selected sub-claim. To avoid losing immediately, Alice must keep the fractional block sensitivity of every decomposition low. So if Bob samples this way at every level, each run of the debate has a non-trivial chance of catching a lying Alice.

Building on this, Bob can amplify his chance of catching Alice through repetition. Since we assume the debaters themselves know the answers to these final, human-judgeable claims, Bob can simply run many debate rollouts on his own, and if he finds one in which Alice made an incorrect human-judgeable claim, he reveals that claim to the judge, so the judge only needs to evaluate a single claim. With enough rollouts, he catches a lying Alice with high probability. Viewed from the lens of practical AI debate, this represents a trade-off between allowing highly sensitive arguments and the inference-time computation required to verify them.

Honesty is the best policy

In FBS Debate, honest play is the best strategy for each debater, no matter what the other does: if the original claim is correct, an honest Alice always wins, and if it is incorrect, an honest Bob wins with overwhelming probability. By contrast, prover-estimator debate only guarantees that for any dishonest strategy Alice picks, Bob has some winning strategy, which can depend on Alice’s strategy in complicated ways. This is a much weaker condition, and in practice training toward the equilibrium of FBS Debate is much more stable and tractable. Furthermore, FBS Debate applies on a worst-case basis: prover-estimator debate only works on average over a distribution of questions, while FBS Debate guarantees that on each individual question, honesty is the best policy.

Optimality

We show that, on each individual question, no protocol that treats human judgment as a black box can find a flawed sub-claim asymptotically more efficiently than FBS Debate.

Discussion and open problems

Debate training is now being applied to frontier-scale models (e.g., Kenton et al., 2026). Our results show that fractional block sensitivity determines how much computational effort any recursive debate protocol must use to ensure an accurate training signal. We believe this is useful for debate experiments even if they don’t use FBS Debate itself. Notably, Bob never needs to decide whether Alice’s sub-claims are true; he only needs to understand the structure of the argument well enough to know where to sample.

Is it possible to design a protocol that goes beyond the fractional block sensitivity barrier we identify? Our lower bounds only apply when human judgment is modeled as a black box. Classical results on interactive proofs show that opening up the black box yields much stronger protocols. These methods seem unlikely to carry over to human judgment: one would essentially need to “read the code” that implements it. Still, some other relaxation of the black-box assumption might lead to better debate protocols.

item.title: Preface to the Computational Agent Theory and ASI Alignment Sequence
item.description:
The idea of “artificial superintelligence [1] ” (ASI) has recently crossed from the realm of science fiction (in the mainstream perception) to the realm of near-term technological goals openly pursued by most leading commercial organizations in the field of AI. Unfortunately, ASI poses a grave existential risk to the human species. This was argued by Eliezer Yudkowsky since 2001 [2] , and by many others (see e.g., Omohundro 2009, Bostrom 2014, Armstrong 2014, Russell 2019, Bengio et al. 2024 (25 authors), Bengio et al. 2025 (13 authors) and Yudkowsky and Soares 2025).

In light of this risk comes the question of how can we make ASI safe [3] . This question is challenging on many levels, because to solve it we need to complete vast gaps in our understanding both in theoretical computer science and in the areas of philosophy concerned with knowledge and decision-making. Moreover, the cost of failure is so enormous that any sane solution has to meet unprecedented standards of reliability and robustness. Not to mention the sociopolitical problem of balance of power in the post-ASI age, something that is out-of-scope for this sequence.

Personally, I started to be concerned with this problem around 2013. In 2018, I created the learning-theoretic AI alignment research agenda (LTA). The LTA combined ideas from MIRI’s agent foundations agenda with the mathematical tools of statistical and computational learning theory in an attempt to create a mathematical theory of intelligent agents. Since then, my collaborators [4] and I have been making steady progress on realizing this vision. In 2023, I wrote an updated overview of the agenda, including a sketch of my proposed alignment protocol: Computational Superimitation. More recently I founded the Computational Rational Agents Laboratory (CORAL), a dedicated research organization [5] .

This year has seen a breakthrough in a key missing piece of LTA: compositional learning theory (see Stringological Sequence Prediction, more on this in following posts). Thanks to this and other insights, we can already see the entire outline of the emerging mathematical framework, one that I named computational agent theory.

In this sequence, I am planning to cover:

  • What is the technical alignment problem and what are its core difficulties, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong.
  • A high-level overview of computational agent theory. This theory differs from other accounts of intelligence and/or rational agency by combining a mature treatment of the relevant philosophical problems (drawing on ideas such as structural realism, computationalism and functional decision theory) with the promise of extracting practical algorithms.
  • How computational agent theory leads to a solution of the technical alignment problem, something that requires a major rethinking of how we design AI systems.
  • The roadmap towards completing the theory, and our current location on this roadmap.
  • Some considerations (scientific, technological and social) about crossing the gap from a theoretical solution to AI alignment to a real-world solution to AI risk.

I thank Jeremy Gillen, Roman Malov, Vinayak Pathak and my beloved spouse @Marcus Ogren for reviewing drafts of this article and making helpful suggestions.

  1. The term “superintelligence” is always used in this sequence to mean “intelligence far beyond that of the smartest humans”. It is never used as the farcical synonym to “artificial intelligence” proposed by Donald Trump. ↩︎

  2. Although Alan Turing warned about machines taking control already around 1951, himself citing a fiction novel by Samuel Butler from 1872. ↩︎

  3. Alternatively, we can ask why should we build ASI at all. In my opinion, it is in humanity’s interest to build ASI eventually, after the problem of safety is investigated so thoroughly as to leave very little room for error. However, our present technological trajectory is extremely far from this ideal, and it would be prudent for world governments to hit the brakes hard. ↩︎

  4. See the names in CORAL’s publication list. ↩︎

  5. Full-time staff currently consists of Alexander Appel, Vinayak Pathak, Matthias Georg Mayer and myself. ↩︎
